business.title: Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer
business.description: Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems. Silicon photonic modulators are central to future high-capacity optical interconnects but face a trade-off between efficiency and bandwidth. This work addresses that challenge using a slow-light modulator with an integrated EO equalizer, enabling 200 Gb/s operation.

science.title: Structure-coefficient theorem for evolutionary games on dynamic networks
science.description: Evolution unfolds in populations of reproducing individuals, with the dynamics shaped by numerous factors, including population structure, update rules, mutation rates, traits (‘strategies’) and the reproductive success derived from traits (‘payoffs’). Developing a unifying principle to predict which traits will evolve and when, remains a major challenge. While rigorous mathematical results exist for static population structures, the general case of dynamic structures, where connections between individuals change over time, is more difficult and less understood. Here we present a structure-coefficient theorem for evolutionary games on dynamic networks with exogenous stochastic transitions. The framework enables arbitrary Markovian network dynamics independent of strategic interactions, together with arbitrary update mechanisms, mutation rates, strategy spaces and payoff matrices. We demonstrate that the combined effects of structure, update rules and mutation on evolutionary outcomes can be fully captured by three universal structure coefficients. Further analysis reveals that, although most sampled dynamic networks do not promote prosocial behavior, a class of dynamic core–periphery networks consistently promotes multiple forms of prosocial behavior, including cooperation, altruism, fairness and trust. The authors establish a structure-coefficient theorem, showing that three universal coefficients capture evolutionary outcomes in changing networks, and identify dynamic core–periphery networks that promote cooperation, altruism, fairness and trust.

science.title: Chemogenetic activation of mitochondria counteracts the Warburg effect in tumor cells
science.description: Upregulation of glycolysis and downregulation of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, termed as the Warburg effect, is characteristic of tumor cells. Restriction of pyruvate flux into the mitochondrial matrix is one of the major mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. Warburg metabolism is beneficial for rapidly proliferating cells; however, the metabolic consequences of activation of mitochondrial respiration in such cells remain unclear. Here we created a chemogenetic instrument, Grubraw, that generates pyruvate from ᴅ-alanine directly in the mitochondrial matrix, bypassing restricted pyruvate influx. In cancer cells, Grubraw-produced mitochondrial pyruvate increased oxidative metabolism. Chemogenetic activation of mitochondria slowed the growth rate of human melanoma xenografts. Moreover, activation of cancer cell mitochondria suppressed the transcription of genes that control cell-cycle progression, cell proliferation and DNA replication. Surprisingly, we found that cancer cells with Warburg metabolism control carbon flux by disposing of excess mitochondrial pyruvate produced by Grubraw and exporting it out of the cell. The chemogenetic tool Grubraw activates mitochondria by generating pyruvate in the mitochondrial matrix. This triggers a genetic switch that slows down tumor cell proliferation. Tumor cells counteract this by exporting excess pyruvate outward.

science.title: Algae-powered soft robot arm uses light to grasp and lift small objects
science.description: Tiny underwater algae sway gently in the current. All of a sudden, a light shines on them and they form robotlike arms that start to pick up small rocks and put them in floating baskets. Sounds like science fiction, but researchers from Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have created a small soft robot arm covered with minuscule algae that can grasp and lift objects. And it's powered by light. This next step in biotechnology has been published in Nature Communications.
